[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#traits)Traits

The [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait is the core API of this crate. It’s intended to be impl’d on values that
may-or-may-not contain secrets, for example the

`zeroize` crate itself defines them on the
core integers e.g. `u8`, `u16`, `i8`, `i16`, as well as arrays thereof. Its core API is
[, a method which takes](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html#tymethod.zeroize)

`Zeroize::zeroize``&mut self` and writes over the type’s internal
memory with some placeholder value, typically some form of `0`.The [ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html) marker trait can be impl’d on types which have a

[impl that can be used for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[. Types which implement this trait receive a blanket impl of the](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`We recommend that types which always contain secrets, and especially ones which need to maintain
complex invariants, do NOT impl the [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait, but instead provide a

[impl which takes care of erasing the secret values from memory directly. Such types can mark that they’re doing this with the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[marker trait. Note that](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroizeOnDrop.html)

`ZeroizeOnDrop`[is](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroizeOnDrop.html)

`ZeroizeOnDrop`*just*a marker trait, and making it actually work requires actually providing a

[impl which takes care of zeroizing secrets.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`Why not impl [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) for such types, e.g. a

`SecretKey` type? The problem is [would effectively leave such types in an invalid state, and a sort of use-after-zeroize condition becomes possible. For that reason, we recommend these types automatically handle zeroization in their](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[handler alone.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/drop/trait.Drop.html)

`Drop`[§](https://docs.rs#supported-types)Supported types

The [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) trait is impl’d on all of Rust’s core scalar types including
integers, floats,

`bool`, and `char`.Additionally, it’s implemented on slices and `IterMut`s of the above types.

When the `alloc` feature is enabled (which it is by default), it’s also
impl’d for `Vec<T>` for the above types as well as `String`, where it provides
[ Vec::clear](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.clear) /

[-like behavior (truncating to zero-length) but ensures the backing memory is securely zeroed with some caveats.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html#method.clear)

`String::clear`With the `std` feature enabled (which it is **not** by default), [ Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)
is also implemented for

[. After calling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ffi/struct.CString.html)

`CString``zeroize()` on a `CString`,
its internal buffer will contain exactly one nul byte. The backing
memory is zeroed by converting it to a `Vec<u8>` and back into a `CString`.
(NOTE: see “Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes” for important `Vec`/`String`/`CString` details)The [ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html) marker trait can be impl’d on types which also
impl

[, which implements](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[by overwriting a value with the default value.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html)

`Zeroize`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derive-support)Custom Derive Support

This crate has custom derive support for the `Zeroize` trait,
gated under the `zeroize` crate’s `zeroize_derive` Cargo feature,
which automatically calls `zeroize()` on all members of a struct
or tuple struct.

Attributes supported for `Zeroize`:

On the item level:

- `#[zeroize(drop)]`:- *deprecated*use- `ZeroizeOnDrop`instead
- `#[zeroize(bound = "T: MyTrait")]`: this replaces any trait bounds inferred by zeroize

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Attributes supported for `ZeroizeOnDrop`:

On the field level:

- `#[zeroize(skip)]`: skips this field or variant when calling- `zeroize()`

Example which derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::{Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop};
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Zeroize, ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which does not derive `Drop` (useful for e.g. `Copy` types)

```
#[cfg(feature = "zeroize_derive")]
use zeroize::Zeroize;
// This struct will *NOT* be zeroized on drop
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Zeroize)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
Example which only derives `Drop`:

```
use zeroize::ZeroizeOnDrop;
// This struct will be zeroized on drop
#[derive(ZeroizeOnDrop)]
struct MyStruct([u8; 32]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#zeroizingz-wrapper-for-zeroizing-arbitrary-values-on-drop)`Zeroizing<Z>`: wrapper for zeroizing arbitrary values on drop

`Zeroizing<Z: Zeroize>` is a generic wrapper type that impls `Deref`
and `DerefMut`, allowing access to an inner value of type `Z`, and also
impls a `Drop` handler which calls `zeroize()` on its contents:

```
use zeroize::Zeroizing;
fn use_secret() {
    let mut secret = Zeroizing::new([0u8; 5]);
    // Set the air shield password
    // Protip (again): don't embed secrets in your source code.
    secret.copy_from_slice(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    assert_eq!(secret.as_ref(), &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
    // The contents of `secret` will be automatically zeroized on drop
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-guarantees-does-this-crate-provide)What guarantees does this crate provide?

This crate guarantees the zeroing operation can’t be “optimized away” by the compiler, as ensured by LLVM’s volatile semantics.

Previously there were worries that the approach used by this crate (mixing volatile and
non-volatile accesses) was undefined behavior due to language contained
in the documentation for `write_volatile`, however after some discussion
within the [Unsafe Code Guidelines Working Group](https://github.com/rust-lang/unsafe-code-guidelines), [these remarks have been removed](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/60972) and the
specific usage pattern in this crate is considered to be well-defined.

All of that said, there is still potential for microarchitectural attacks (ala Spectre/Meltdown) to leak “zeroized” secrets through covert channels. This crate makes no guarantees that zeroized values cannot be leaked through such channels, as they represent flaws in the underlying hardware.

[§](https://docs.rs#stackheap-zeroing-notes)Stack/Heap Zeroing Notes

This crate can be used to zero values from either the stack or the heap. We recommend storing sensitive data on the heap whenever possible to reduce the potential for making copies in memory via Rust move semantics, however note that stack spilling and other optimizations may leave temporary copies of data from the heap on the stack.

[ zeroize_stack](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroize_stack.html) can be used to zeroize stack memory.

[ Pin](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/pin/struct.Pin.html) can be leveraged in conjunction with this crate to ensure data kept
on the stack isn’t moved.

The `Zeroize` impls for `Vec`, `String` and `CString` zeroize the entire capacity of their
backing buffer, but cannot guarantee copies of the data were not previously made by buffer
reallocation. It’s therefore important when attempting to zeroize such buffers to initialize
them to the correct capacity, and take care to prevent subsequent reallocation.

The [ secrecy](https://docs.rs/secrecy) crate provides higher-level abstractions for eliminating
usage patterns which can cause reallocations:

[§](https://docs.rs#what-about-clearing-registers-mlock-mprotect-etc)What about: clearing registers, `mlock()`, `mprotect()`, etc?

This crate is focused on providing simple, unobtrusive support for reliably zeroing memory using the best approach possible on stable Rust.

Clearing registers is a difficult problem that can’t easily be solved by
something like a crate, and requires either inline ASM or rustc support.
See [https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/17046) for background on
this particular problem.

Other memory protection mechanisms are interesting and useful, but often overkill (e.g. defending against RAM scraping or attackers with swap access). In as much as there may be merit to these approaches, there are also many other crates that already implement more sophisticated memory protections. Such protections are explicitly out-of-scope for this crate.

Zeroing memory is [good cryptographic hygiene](https://github.com/veorq/cryptocoding#clean-memory-of-secret-data) and this crate seeks to promote
it in the most unobtrusive manner possible. This includes omitting complex
`unsafe` memory protection systems and just trying to make the best memory
zeroing crate available.

# openssl - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openssl/^0.10/

## Expand description

Bindings to OpenSSL

This crate provides a safe interface to the popular OpenSSL cryptography library. OpenSSL versions 1.0.2 through 4.x.x and LibreSSL versions 3.5 through 4.3.x are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#building)Building

Both OpenSSL libraries and headers are required to build this crate. There are multiple options available to locate OpenSSL.

[§](https://docs.rs#vendored)Vendored

If the `vendored` Cargo feature is enabled, the `openssl-src` crate will be used to compile and statically link to
a copy of OpenSSL. The build process requires a C compiler, perl (and perl-core), and make. The OpenSSL version will generally track
the newest OpenSSL release, and changes to the version are *not* considered breaking changes.

```
[dependencies]
openssl = { version = "0.10", features = ["vendored"] }
```
The vendored copy will be configured to automatically find a configuration and root certificates at `/usr/local/ssl`.
This path can be overridden with an environment variable (see the manual section below).
Alternatively, the `openssl-probe` crate can be used to find root certificates at runtime.

[§](https://docs.rs#automatic)Automatic

The `openssl-sys` crate will automatically detect OpenSSL installations via Homebrew on macOS and vcpkg on Windows.
Additionally, it will use `pkg-config` on Unix-like systems to find the system installation.

```
# macOS (Homebrew)
$ brew install openssl@4
# macOS (MacPorts)
$ sudo port install openssl
# macOS (pkgsrc)
$ sudo pkgin install openssl
# Arch Linux
$ sudo pacman -S pkgconf openssl
# Debian and Ubuntu
$ sudo apt-get install pkg-config libssl-dev
# Fedora
$ sudo dnf install pkgconf perl-FindBin perl-IPC-Cmd openssl-devel
# Alpine Linux
$ apk add pkgconf openssl-dev
# openSUSE
$ sudo zypper in libopenssl-devel
```
[§](https://docs.rs#manual)Manual

A set of environment variables can be used to point `openssl-sys` towards an OpenSSL installation. They will
override the automatic detection logic.

- `OPENSSL_DIR`- If specified, the directory of an OpenSSL installation. The directory should contain- `lib`and- `include`subdirectories containing the libraries and headers respectively.
- `OPENSSL_LIB_DIR`and- `OPENSSL_INCLUDE_DIR`- If specified, the directories containing the OpenSSL libraries and headers respectively. This can be used if the OpenSSL installation is split in a nonstandard directory layout.
- `OPENSSL_STATIC`- If set, the crate will statically link to OpenSSL rather than dynamically link.
- `OPENSSL_LIBS`- If set, a- `:`-separated list of library names to link to (e.g.- `ssl:crypto`). This can be used if nonstandard library names were used for whatever reason.
- `OPENSSL_NO_VENDOR`- If set, always find OpenSSL in the system, even if the- `vendored`feature is enabled.

If the `vendored` Cargo feature is enabled, the following environment variable can also be used to further configure
the OpenSSL build.

- `OPENSSL_CONFIG_DIR`- If set, the copy of OpenSSL built by the- `openssl-src`crate will be configured to look for configuration files and root certificates in this directory.

Additionally, these variables can be prefixed with the upper-cased target architecture (e.g.
`X86_64_UNKNOWN_LINUX_GNU_OPENSSL_DIR`), which can be useful when cross compiling.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-detection)Feature Detection

APIs have been added to and removed from the various supported OpenSSL versions, and this library exposes the functionality available in the version being linked against. This means that methods, constants, and even modules will be present when building against one version of OpenSSL but not when building against another! APIs will document any version-specific availability restrictions.

A build script can be used to detect the OpenSSL or LibreSSL version at compile time if needed. The `openssl-sys`
crate propagates the version via the `DEP_OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER` and `DEP_OPENSSL_LIBRESSL_VERSION_NUMBER`
environment variables to build scripts. The version format is a hex-encoding of the OpenSSL release version:
`0xMNNFFPPS`. For example, version 1.0.2g’s encoding is `0x1_00_02_07_0`.

For example, let’s say we want to adjust the TLSv1.3 cipher suites used by a client, but also want to compile against OpenSSL versions that don’t support TLSv1.3:

Cargo.toml:

```
[dependencies]
openssl-sys = "0.9"
openssl = "0.10"
```
build.rs:

```
use std::env;
fn main() {
    if let Ok(v) = env::var("DEP_OPENSSL_VERSION_NUMBER") {
        let version = u64::from_str_radix(&v, 16).unwrap();
        if version >= 0x1_01_01_00_0 {
            println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=openssl111");
        }
    }
}
```
lib.rs:

```
use openssl::ssl::{SslConnector, SslMethod};
let mut ctx = SslConnector::builder(SslMethod::tls()).unwrap();
// set_ciphersuites was added in OpenSSL 1.1.1, so we can only call it when linking against that version
#[cfg(openssl111)]
ctx.set_ciphersuites("TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256").unwrap();
```

# rcgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rcgen/latest/target-redirect/rcgen/

## Expand description

Rust X.509 certificate generation utility

This crate provides a way to generate self signed X.509 certificates.

The most simple way of using this crate is by calling the
[ generate_simple_self_signed](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_simple_self_signed.html) function.
For more customization abilities, construct a

[and a key pair to call](https://docs.rs/struct.CertificateParams.html)

`CertificateParams`[or](https://docs.rs/struct.CertificateParams.html#method.signed_by)

`CertificateParams::signed_by()`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.CertificateParams.html#method.self_signed)

`CertificateParams::self_signed()`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rcgen::{generate_simple_self_signed, CertifiedKey};
// Generate a certificate that's valid for "localhost" and "hello.world.example"
let subject_alt_names = vec!["hello.world.example".to_string(),
	"localhost".to_string()];
let CertifiedKey { cert, signing_key } = generate_simple_self_signed(subject_alt_names).unwrap();
println!("{}", cert.pem());
println!("{}", signing_key.serialize_pem());
```

# rustls_pki_types - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/index.html

## Expand description

This crate provides types for representing X.509 certificates, keys and other types as
commonly used in the rustls ecosystem. It is intended to be used by crates that need to work
with such X.509 types, such as [rustls](https://crates.io/crates/rustls),
[rustls-webpki](https://crates.io/crates/rustls-webpki), and others.

Some of these crates used to define their own trivial wrappers around DER-encoded bytes. However, in order to avoid inconvenient dependency edges, these were all disconnected. By using a common low-level crate of types with long-term stable API, we hope to avoid the downsides of unnecessary dependency edges while providing good interoperability between crates.

[§](https://docs.rs#der-and-pem)DER and PEM

Many of the types defined in this crate represent DER-encoded data. DER is a binary encoding of the ASN.1 format commonly used in web PKI specifications. It is a binary encoding, so it is relatively compact when stored in memory. However, as a binary format, it is not very easy to work with for humans and in contexts where binary data is inconvenient. For this reason, many tools and protocols use a ASCII-based encoding of DER, called PEM. In addition to the base64-encoded DER, PEM objects are delimited by header and footer lines which indicate the type of object contained in the PEM blob.

Types here can be created from:

- DER using (for example) `PrivatePkcs8KeyDer::from()`
- PEM using (for example) `pem::PemObject::from_pem_slice()`

The [ pem::PemObject](https://docs.rs/pem/trait.PemObject.html) trait contains the full selection of ways to construct
these types from PEM encodings.  That includes ways to open and read from a file,
from a slice, or from an

`std::io` stream.There is also a lower-level API that allows a given PEM file to be fully consumed
in one pass, even if it contains different data types: see the implementation of
the [ pem::PemObject](https://docs.rs/pem/trait.PemObject.html) trait on the

`(pem::SectionKind, Vec<u8>)` tuple.[§](https://docs.rs#creating-new-certificates-and-keys)Creating new certificates and keys

This crate does not provide any functionality for creating new certificates or keys. However,
the [rcgen](https://docs.rs/rcgen) crate can be used to create new certificates and keys.

[§](https://docs.rs#cloning-private-keys)Cloning private keys

This crate intentionally **does not** implement `Clone` on private key types in
order to minimize the exposure of private key data in memory.

If you want to extend the lifetime of a `PrivateKeyDer<'_>`, consider [ PrivateKeyDer::clone_key()](https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/enum.PrivateKeyDer.html#method.clone_key).
Alternatively  since these types are immutable, consider wrapping the

`PrivateKeyDer<'_>` in a [or an](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/struct.Rc.html)

`Rc`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[§](https://docs.rs#target-wasm32-unknown-unknown-with-the-web-feature)Target `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with the `web` feature

[ std::time::SystemTime](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html)
is unavailable in

`wasm32-unknown-unknown` targets, so calls to
[, otherwise enabled by the](https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/struct.UnixTime.html#method.now)

`UnixTime::now()`[feature, require building instead with the](https://docs.rs/crate/rustls-pki-types/latest/features#std)

`std`[feature. It gets time by calling](https://docs.rs/crate/rustls-pki-types/latest/features#web)

`web`[in the browser.](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/now)

`Date.now()`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use alg_id::`- [AlgorithmIdentifier](https://docs.rs/alg_id/struct.AlgorithmIdentifier.html);

# rustls_pki_types/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! This crate provides types for representing X.509 certificates, keys and other types as
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! commonly used in the rustls ecosystem. It is intended to be used by crates that need to work
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! with such X.509 types, such as [rustls](https://crates.io/crates/rustls),
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [rustls-webpki](https://crates.io/crates/rustls-webpki), and others.
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!

[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! However, in order to avoid inconvenient dependency edges, these were all disconnected. By
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! using a common low-level crate of types with long-term stable API, we hope to avoid the
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! downsides of unnecessary dependency edges while providing good interoperability between crates.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//!
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! ## DER and PEM
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! Many of the types defined in this crate represent DER-encoded data. DER is a binary encoding of
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! the ASN.1 format commonly used in web PKI specifications. It is a binary encoding, so it is
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! relatively compact when stored in memory. However, as a binary format, it is not very easy to
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! work with for humans and in contexts where binary data is inconvenient. For this reason,
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! many tools and protocols use a ASCII-based encoding of DER, called PEM. In addition to the
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! base64-encoded DER, PEM objects are delimited by header and footer lines which indicate the type
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! of object contained in the PEM blob.
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! Types here can be created from:
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! - DER using (for example) [`PrivatePkcs8KeyDer::from()`].
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! - PEM using (for example) [`pem::PemObject::from_pem_slice()`].

[93](https://docs.rs#93)/// Low-level PEM decoding APIs.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)///
[95](https://docs.rs#95)/// These APIs allow decoding PEM format in an iterator, which means you
[96](https://docs.rs#96)/// can load multiple different types of PEM section from a file in a single
[97](https://docs.rs#97)/// pass.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[99](https://docs.rs#99)pub mod pem;
[100](https://docs.rs#100)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)pub use alg_id::AlgorithmIdentifier;
[102](https://docs.rs#102)pub use server_name::{
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    AddrParseError, DnsName, InvalidDnsNameError, IpAddr, Ipv4Addr, Ipv6Addr, ServerName,
[104](https://docs.rs#104)};
[105](https://docs.rs#105)
[106](https://docs.rs#106)/// A DER-encoded X.509 private key, in one of several formats
[107](https://docs.rs#107)///
[108](https://docs.rs#108)/// See variant inner types for more detailed information.
[109](https://docs.rs#109)///
[110](https://docs.rs#110)/// This can load several types of PEM-encoded private key, and then reveal
[111](https://docs.rs#111)/// which types were found:
[112](https://docs.rs#112)///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)/// ```rust
[114](https://docs.rs#114)/// # #[cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))] {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)/// use rustls_pki_types::{PrivateKeyDer, pem::PemObject};
[116](https://docs.rs#116)///
[117](https://docs.rs#117)/// // load from a PEM file
[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// let pkcs8 = PrivateKeyDer::from_pem_file("tests/data/nistp256key.pkcs8.pem").unwrap();
[119](https://docs.rs#119)/// let pkcs1 = PrivateKeyDer::from_pem_file("tests/data/rsa1024.pkcs1.pem").unwrap();
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// let sec1 = PrivateKeyDer::from_pem_file("tests/data/nistp256key.pem").unwrap();
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// assert!(matches!(pkcs8, PrivateKeyDer::Pkcs8(_)));
[122](https://docs.rs#122)/// assert!(matches!(pkcs1, PrivateKeyDer::Pkcs1(_)));
[123](https://docs.rs#123)/// assert!(matches!(sec1, PrivateKeyDer::Sec1(_)));
[124](https://docs.rs#124)/// # }
[125](https://docs.rs#125)/// ```
[126](https://docs.rs#126)#[non_exhaustive]
[127](https://docs.rs#127)#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
[128](https://docs.rs#128)pub enum PrivateKeyDer<'a> {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    /// An RSA private key
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    Pkcs1(PrivatePkcs1KeyDer<'a>),
[131](https://docs.rs#131)    /// A Sec1 private key
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    Sec1(PrivateSec1KeyDer<'a>),
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    /// A PKCS#8 private key
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    Pkcs8(PrivatePkcs8KeyDer<'a>),
[135](https://docs.rs#135)}
[136](https://docs.rs#136)

[141](https://docs.rs#141)            Self::Pkcs1(key) => key.zeroize(),
[142](https://docs.rs#142)            Self::Sec1(key) => key.zeroize(),
[143](https://docs.rs#143)            Self::Pkcs8(key) => key.zeroize(),
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        }

[200](https://docs.rs#200)impl<'a> TryFrom<&'a [u8]> for PrivateKeyDer<'a> {
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    type Error = &'static str;
[202](https://docs.rs#202)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    fn try_from(key: &'a [u8]) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)        const SHORT_FORM_LEN_MAX: u8 = 128;
[205](https://docs.rs#205)        const TAG_SEQUENCE: u8 = 0x30;
[206](https://docs.rs#206)        const TAG_INTEGER: u8 = 0x02;
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)        // We expect all key formats to begin with a SEQUENCE, which requires at least 2 bytes
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        // in the short length encoding.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        if key.first() != Some(&TAG_SEQUENCE) || key.len() < 2 {
[211](https://docs.rs#211)            return Err(INVALID_KEY_DER_ERR);
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        }
[213](https://docs.rs#213)
[214](https://docs.rs#214)        // The length of the SEQUENCE is encoded in the second byte. We must skip this many bytes.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        let skip_len = match key[1] >= SHORT_FORM_LEN_MAX {
[216](https://docs.rs#216)            // 1 byte for SEQUENCE tag, 1 byte for short-form len
[217](https://docs.rs#217)            false => 2,
[218](https://docs.rs#218)            // 1 byte for SEQUENCE tag, 1 byte for start of len, remaining bytes encoded
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            // in key[1].
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            true => 2 + (key[1] - SHORT_FORM_LEN_MAX) as usize,
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        };
[222](https://docs.rs#222)        let key_bytes = key.get(skip_len..).ok_or(INVALID_KEY_DER_ERR)?;
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)        // PKCS#8 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5208) describes the PrivateKeyInfo
[225](https://docs.rs#225)        // structure as:
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        //   PrivateKeyInfo ::= SEQUENCE {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        //      version Version,
[228](https://docs.rs#228)        //      privateKeyAlgorithm AlgorithmIdentifier {{PrivateKeyAlgorithms}},
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        //      privateKey PrivateKey,
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        //      attributes [0] Attributes OPTIONAL
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        //   }
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        // PKCS#5 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018) describes the AlgorithmIdentifier
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        // as a SEQUENCE.
[234](https://docs.rs#234)        //
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        // Therefore, we consider the outer SEQUENCE, a version number, and the start of
[236](https://docs.rs#236)        // an AlgorithmIdentifier to be enough to identify a PKCS#8 key. If it were PKCS#1 or SEC1
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        // the version would not be followed by a SEQUENCE.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        if matches!(key_bytes, [TAG_INTEGER, 0x01, _, TAG_SEQUENCE, ..]) {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            return Ok(Self::Pkcs8(key.into()));
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        }
[241](https://docs.rs#241)
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        // PKCS#1 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017) describes the RSAPrivateKey structure
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        // as:
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        //  RSAPrivateKey ::= SEQUENCE {
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        //              version           Version,
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        //              modulus           INTEGER,  -- n
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        //              publicExponent    INTEGER,  -- e
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        //              privateExponent   INTEGER,  -- d
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        //              prime1            INTEGER,  -- p
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        //              prime2            INTEGER,  -- q
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        //              exponent1         INTEGER,  -- d mod (p-1)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        //              exponent2         INTEGER,  -- d mod (q-1)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        //              coefficient       INTEGER,  -- (inverse of q) mod p
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        //              otherPrimeInfos   OtherPrimeInfos OPTIONAL
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        //          }
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        //
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        // Therefore, we consider the outer SEQUENCE and a Version of 0 to be enough to identify
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        // a PKCS#1 key. If it were PKCS#8, the version would be followed by a SEQUENCE. If it
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        // were SEC1, the VERSION would have been 1.
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        if key_bytes.starts_with(&[TAG_INTEGER, 0x01, 0x00]) {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)            return Ok(Self::Pkcs1(key.into()));
[262](https://docs.rs#262)        }
[263](https://docs.rs#263)
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        // SEC1 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5915) describes the ECPrivateKey structure as:
[265](https://docs.rs#265)        //   ECPrivateKey ::= SEQUENCE {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        //      version        INTEGER { ecPrivkeyVer1(1) } (ecPrivkeyVer1),
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        //      privateKey     OCTET STRING,
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        //      parameters [0] ECParameters {{ NamedCurve }} OPTIONAL,
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        //      publicKey  [1] BIT STRING OPTIONAL
[270](https://docs.rs#270)        //   }
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        //
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        // Therefore, we consider the outer SEQUENCE and an INTEGER of 1 to be enough to
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        // identify a SEC1 key. If it were PKCS#8 or PKCS#1, the version would have been 0.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        if key_bytes.starts_with(&[TAG_INTEGER, 0x01, 0x01]) {
[275](https://docs.rs#275)            return Ok(Self::Sec1(key.into()));
[276](https://docs.rs#276)        }
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        Err(INVALID_KEY_DER_ERR)
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    }
[280](https://docs.rs#280)}
[281](https://docs.rs#281)
[282](https://docs.rs#282)static INVALID_KEY_DER_ERR: &str = "unknown or invalid key format";
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[285](https://docs.rs#285)impl TryFrom<Vec<u8>> for PrivateKeyDer<'_> {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    type Error = &'static str;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    fn try_from(key: Vec<u8>) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
[289](https://docs.rs#289)        Ok(match PrivateKeyDer::try_from(&key[..])? {
[290](https://docs.rs#290)            PrivateKeyDer::Pkcs1(_) => Self::Pkcs1(key.into()),
[291](https://docs.rs#291)            PrivateKeyDer::Sec1(_) => Self::Sec1(key.into()),
[292](https://docs.rs#292)            PrivateKeyDer::Pkcs8(_) => Self::Pkcs8(key.into()),
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        })
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    }

[498](https://docs.rs#498)/// A trust anchor (a.k.a. root CA)
[499](https://docs.rs#499)///
[500](https://docs.rs#500)/// Traditionally, certificate verification libraries have represented trust anchors as full X.509
[501](https://docs.rs#501)/// root certificates. However, those certificates contain a lot more data than is needed for
[502](https://docs.rs#502)/// verifying certificates. The [`TrustAnchor`] representation allows an application to store
[503](https://docs.rs#503)/// just the essential elements of trust anchors.
[504](https://docs.rs#504)///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// The most common way to get one of these is to call [`rustls_webpki::anchor_from_trusted_cert()`].
[506](https://docs.rs#506)///
[507](https://docs.rs#507)/// [`rustls_webpki::anchor_from_trusted_cert()`]: https://docs.rs/rustls-webpki/latest/webpki/fn.anchor_from_trusted_cert.html
[508](https://docs.rs#508)#[allow(clippy::exhaustive_structs)]
[509](https://docs.rs#509)#[derive(Clone, Debug, Hash, PartialEq, Eq)]
[510](https://docs.rs#510)pub struct TrustAnchor<'a> {
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// Value of the `subject` field of the trust anchor
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    pub subject: Der<'a>,
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// Value of the `subjectPublicKeyInfo` field of the trust anchor
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    pub subject_public_key_info: Der<'a>,
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    /// Value of DER-encoded `NameConstraints`, containing name constraints to the trust anchor, if any
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    pub name_constraints: Option<Der<'a>>,
[517](https://docs.rs#517)}
[518](https://docs.rs#518)
[519](https://docs.rs#519)impl TrustAnchor<'_> {
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    /// Yield a `'static` lifetime of the `TrustAnchor` by allocating owned `Der` variants
[521](https://docs.rs#521)    #[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    pub fn to_owned(&self) -> TrustAnchor<'static> {
[523](https://docs.rs#523)        #[cfg(not(feature = "std"))]
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        use alloc::borrow::ToOwned;
[525](https://docs.rs#525)        TrustAnchor {
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            subject: self.subject.as_ref().to_owned().into(),
[527](https://docs.rs#527)            subject_public_key_info: self.subject_public_key_info.as_ref().to_owned().into(),
[528](https://docs.rs#528)            name_constraints: self
[529](https://docs.rs#529)                .name_constraints
[530](https://docs.rs#530)                .as_ref()
[531](https://docs.rs#531)                .map(|nc| nc.as_ref().to_owned().into()),
[532](https://docs.rs#532)        }
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    }
[534](https://docs.rs#534)}

[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// A Certificate Revocation List; as specified in RFC 5280

[542](https://docs.rs#542)/// # #[cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))] {

[544](https://docs.rs#544)///
[545](https://docs.rs#545)/// // load several from a PEM file
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// let crls: Vec<_> = CertificateRevocationListDer::pem_file_iter("tests/data/crl.pem")
[547](https://docs.rs#547)///     .unwrap()
[548](https://docs.rs#548)///     .collect();
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// assert!(crls.len() >= 1);

[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// // or one from a PEM byte slice...

[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// CertificateRevocationListDer::from_pem_slice(byte_slice).unwrap();
[554](https://docs.rs#554)///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// // or several from a PEM byte slice
[556](https://docs.rs#556)/// let crls: Vec<_> = CertificateRevocationListDer::pem_slice_iter(byte_slice)
[557](https://docs.rs#557)///     .collect();
[558](https://docs.rs#558)/// assert!(crls.len() >= 1);
[559](https://docs.rs#559)/// # }
[560](https://docs.rs#560)/// ```

[803](https://docs.rs#803)    /// Convert an iterator over PEM items into an `EchConfigListBytes` and private key.
[804](https://docs.rs#804)    ///
[805](https://docs.rs#805)    /// This handles the "ECHConfig file" format specified in
[806](https://docs.rs#806)    /// <https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-farrell-tls-pemesni-05.html#name-echconfig-file>
[807](https://docs.rs#807)    ///
[808](https://docs.rs#808)    /// Use it like:
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    ///
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    /// ```rust
[811](https://docs.rs#811)    /// # #[cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))] {
[812](https://docs.rs#812)    /// # use rustls_pki_types::{EchConfigListBytes, pem::PemObject};
[813](https://docs.rs#813)    /// let (config, key) = EchConfigListBytes::config_and_key_from_iter(
[814](https://docs.rs#814)    ///     PemObject::pem_file_iter("tests/data/ech.pem").unwrap()
[815](https://docs.rs#815)    /// ).unwrap();
[816](https://docs.rs#816)    /// # }
[817](https://docs.rs#817)    /// ```
[818](https://docs.rs#818)    pub fn config_and_key_from_iter(
[819](https://docs.rs#819)        iter: impl Iterator<Item = Result<(SectionKind, Vec<u8>), pem::Error>>,
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    ) -> Result<(Self, PrivatePkcs8KeyDer<'static>), pem::Error> {
[821](https://docs.rs#821)        let mut key = None;
[822](https://docs.rs#822)        let mut config = None;
[823](https://docs.rs#823)
[824](https://docs.rs#824)        for item in iter {
[825](https://docs.rs#825)            let (kind, data) = item?;
[826](https://docs.rs#826)            match kind {
[827](https://docs.rs#827)                SectionKind::PrivateKey => {
[828](https://docs.rs#828)                    key = PrivatePkcs8KeyDer::from_pem(kind, data);
[829](https://docs.rs#829)                }
[830](https://docs.rs#830)                SectionKind::EchConfigList => {
[831](https://docs.rs#831)                    config = Self::from_pem(kind, data);
[832](https://docs.rs#832)                }
[833](https://docs.rs#833)                _ => continue,
[834](https://docs.rs#834)            };
[835](https://docs.rs#835)
[836](https://docs.rs#836)            if let (Some(_key), Some(_config)) = (&key, &config) {
[837](https://docs.rs#837)                return Ok((config.take().unwrap(), key.take().unwrap()));
[838](https://docs.rs#838)            }
[839](https://docs.rs#839)        }
[840](https://docs.rs#840)
[841](https://docs.rs#841)        Err(pem::Error::NoItemsFound)
[842](https://docs.rs#842)    }

[883](https://docs.rs#883)/// An abstract signature verification algorithm.
[884](https://docs.rs#884)///
[885](https://docs.rs#885)/// One of these is needed per supported pair of public key type (identified
[886](https://docs.rs#886)/// with `public_key_alg_id()`) and `signatureAlgorithm` (identified with
[887](https://docs.rs#887)/// `signature_alg_id()`).  Note that both of these `AlgorithmIdentifier`s include
[888](https://docs.rs#888)/// the parameters encoding, so separate `SignatureVerificationAlgorithm`s are needed
[889](https://docs.rs#889)/// for each possible public key or signature parameters.
[890](https://docs.rs#890)///
[891](https://docs.rs#891)/// Debug implementations should list the public key algorithm identifier and
[892](https://docs.rs#892)/// signature algorithm identifier in human friendly form (i.e. not encoded bytes),
[893](https://docs.rs#893)/// along with the name of the implementing library (to distinguish different
[894](https://docs.rs#894)/// implementations of the same algorithms).
[895](https://docs.rs#895)pub trait SignatureVerificationAlgorithm: Send + Sync + fmt::Debug {
[896](https://docs.rs#896)    /// Verify a signature.
[897](https://docs.rs#897)    ///
[898](https://docs.rs#898)    /// `public_key` is the `subjectPublicKey` value from a `SubjectPublicKeyInfo` encoding
[899](https://docs.rs#899)    /// and is untrusted.  The key's `subjectPublicKeyInfo` matches the [`AlgorithmIdentifier`]
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    /// returned by `public_key_alg_id()`.
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    ///
[902](https://docs.rs#902)    /// `message` is the data over which the signature was allegedly computed.
[903](https://docs.rs#903)    /// It is not hashed; implementations of this trait function must do hashing
[904](https://docs.rs#904)    /// if that is required by the algorithm they implement.
[905](https://docs.rs#905)    ///
[906](https://docs.rs#906)    /// `signature` is the signature allegedly over `message`.
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    ///
[908](https://docs.rs#908)    /// Return `Ok(())` only if `signature` is a valid signature on `message`.
[909](https://docs.rs#909)    ///
[910](https://docs.rs#910)    /// Return `Err(InvalidSignature)` if the signature is invalid, including if the `public_key`
[911](https://docs.rs#911)    /// encoding is invalid.  There is no need or opportunity to produce errors
[912](https://docs.rs#912)    /// that are more specific than this.
[913](https://docs.rs#913)    fn verify_signature(
[914](https://docs.rs#914)        &self,
[915](https://docs.rs#915)        public_key: &[u8],
[916](https://docs.rs#916)        message: &[u8],
[917](https://docs.rs#917)        signature: &[u8],
[918](https://docs.rs#918)    ) -> Result<(), InvalidSignature>;
[919](https://docs.rs#919)
[920](https://docs.rs#920)    /// Return the `AlgorithmIdentifier` that must equal a public key's
[921](https://docs.rs#921)    /// `subjectPublicKeyInfo` value for this `SignatureVerificationAlgorithm`
[922](https://docs.rs#922)    /// to be used for signature verification.
[923](https://docs.rs#923)    fn public_key_alg_id(&self) -> AlgorithmIdentifier;
[924](https://docs.rs#924)
[925](https://docs.rs#925)    /// Return the `AlgorithmIdentifier` that must equal the `signatureAlgorithm` value
[926](https://docs.rs#926)    /// on the data to be verified for this `SignatureVerificationAlgorithm` to be used
[927](https://docs.rs#927)    /// for signature verification.
[928](https://docs.rs#928)    fn signature_alg_id(&self) -> AlgorithmIdentifier;
[929](https://docs.rs#929)
[930](https://docs.rs#930)    /// Return the FIPS status of this algorithm or implementation.
[931](https://docs.rs#931)    fn fips_status(&self) -> FipsStatus {
[932](https://docs.rs#932)        match self.fips() {
[933](https://docs.rs#933)            true => FipsStatus::Pending,
[934](https://docs.rs#934)            false => FipsStatus::Unvalidated,
[935](https://docs.rs#935)        }
[936](https://docs.rs#936)    }
[937](https://docs.rs#937)
[938](https://docs.rs#938)    /// Return `true` if this is backed by a FIPS-approved implementation.
[939](https://docs.rs#939)    fn fips(&self) -> bool {
[940](https://docs.rs#940)        false
[941](https://docs.rs#941)    }
[942](https://docs.rs#942)}

[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)// Format an iterator of u8 into a hex string
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)fn hex<'a>(f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>, payload: impl IntoIterator<Item = &'a u8>) -> fmt::Result {
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)    for (i, b) in payload.into_iter().enumerate() {
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)        if i == 0 {
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)            write!(f, "0x")?;
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)        }
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)        write!(f, "{b:02x}")?;
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)    }
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)    Ok(())

[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)    fn bytes_inner_equality() {
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)        let owned_a = BytesInner::Owned(vec![1, 2, 3]);
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)        let owned_b = BytesInner::Owned(vec![4, 5]);
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)        let borrowed_a = BytesInner::Borrowed(&[1, 2, 3]);
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)        let borrowed_b = BytesInner::Borrowed(&[99]);
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)
[1150](https://docs.rs#1150)        // Self-equality.
[1151](https://docs.rs#1151)        assert_eq!(owned_a, owned_a);
[1152](https://docs.rs#1152)        assert_eq!(owned_b, owned_b);
[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)        assert_eq!(borrowed_a, borrowed_a);
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)        assert_eq!(borrowed_b, borrowed_b);
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)        // Borrowed vs Owned equality
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)        assert_eq!(owned_a, borrowed_a);
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)        assert_eq!(borrowed_a, owned_a);
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)        // Owned inequality
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)        assert_ne!(owned_a, owned_b);
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)        assert_ne!(owned_b, owned_a);
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)        // Borrowed inequality
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)        assert_ne!(borrowed_a, borrowed_b);
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)        assert_ne!(borrowed_b, borrowed_a);
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)
[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)        // Borrowed vs Owned inequality
[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)        assert_ne!(owned_a, borrowed_b);
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)        assert_ne!(borrowed_b, owned_a);
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)    }

`pub struct PrivatePkcs1KeyDer<'a>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A DER-encoded plaintext RSA private key; as specified in PKCS#1/RFC 3447

RSA private keys are identified in PEM context as `RSA PRIVATE KEY` and when stored in a
file usually use a `.pem` or `.key` extension.

`alloc`## Expand description

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Certificate)

### Certificate

A DER-encoded x509 certificate.

Appears as “CERTIFICATE” in PEM files.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PublicKey)

### PublicKey

A DER-encoded Subject Public Key Info; as specified in RFC 7468.

Appears as “PUBLIC KEY” in PEM files.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RsaPrivateKey)

### RsaPrivateKey

A DER-encoded plaintext RSA private key; as specified in PKCS #1/RFC 3447

Appears as “RSA PRIVATE KEY” in PEM files.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PrivateKey)

### PrivateKey

A DER-encoded plaintext private key; as specified in PKCS #8/RFC 5958

Appears as “PRIVATE KEY” in PEM files.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EcPrivateKey)

### EcPrivateKey

A Sec1-encoded plaintext private key; as specified in RFC 5915

Appears as “EC PRIVATE KEY” in PEM files.

[242](#242)    line: &mut Vec<u8>,
[243](#243)    b64buf: &mut Vec<u8>,
[244](#244)) -> Result<Option<(SectionKind, Vec<u8>)>, Error> {

[248](#248)        let len = read_until_newline(rd, line).map_err(Error::Io)?;
[249](#249)
[250](#250)        let next_line = if len == 0 {
[251](#251)            None
[252](#252)        } else {
[253](#253)            Some(line.as_slice())
[254](#254)        };
[255](#255)
[256](#256)        match read(next_line, &mut section, b64buf) {
[257](#257)            Ok(ControlFlow::Break(opt)) => return Ok(opt),
[258](#258)            Ok(ControlFlow::Continue(())) => continue,
[259](#259)            Err(e) => return Err(e),
[260](#260)        }

[264](#264)#[allow(clippy::type_complexity)]
[265](#265)fn read(
[266](#266)    next_line: Option<&[u8]>,
[267](#267)    section: &mut Option<SectionLabel>,
[268](#268)    b64buf: &mut Vec<u8>,
[269](#269)) -> Result<ControlFlow<Option<(SectionKind, Vec<u8>)>, ()>, Error> {
[270](#270)    let line = if let Some(line) = next_line {
[271](#271)        line
[272](#272)    } else {
[273](#273)        return match section.take() {
[275](#275)            Some(label) => Err(Error::MissingSectionEnd {
[276](#276)                end_marker: label.as_ref().to_vec(),
[277](#277)            }),
[278](#278)            None => Ok(ControlFlow::Break(None)),
[279](#279)        };
[280](#280)    };
[281](#281)
[282](#282)    if line.starts_with(b"-----BEGIN ") {
[283](#283)        let (mut trailer, mut pos) = (0, line.len());
[284](#284)        for (i, &b) in line.iter().enumerate().rev() {
[285](#285)            match b {
[286](#286)                b'-' => {
[287](#287)                    trailer += 1;
[288](#288)                    pos = i;
[289](#289)                }
[290](#290)                b'\n' | b'\r' | b' ' => continue,
[291](#291)                _ => break,
[292](#292)            }
[293](#293)        }
[294](#294)
[295](#295)        if trailer != 5 {
[296](#296)            return Err(Error::IllegalSectionStart {
[297](#297)                line: line.to_vec(),
[298](#298)            });
[299](#299)        }
[300](#300)
[301](#301)        let ty = &line[11..pos];
[302](#302)        *section = Some(SectionLabel::from(ty));
[303](#303)        return Ok(ControlFlow::Continue(()));
[304](#304)    }
[305](#305)
[306](#306)    if let Some(label) = section.as_ref() {
[307](#307)        if label.is_end(line) {
[308](#308)            let kind = match label {
[309](#309)                SectionLabel::Known(kind) => *kind,
[310](#310)                SectionLabel::Unknown(_) => {
[312](#312)                    *section = None;
[313](#313)                    b64buf.clear();
[314](#314)                    return Ok(ControlFlow::Continue(()));
[315](#315)                }
[316](#316)            };
[317](#317)
[318](#318)            let mut der = vec![0u8; base64::decoded_length(b64buf.len())];
[319](#319)            let der_len = match kind.secret() {
[320](#320)                true => base64::decode_secret(b64buf, &mut der),
[321](#321)                false => base64::decode_public(b64buf, &mut der),
[322](#322)            }
[323](#323)            .map_err(|err| Error::Base64Decode(format!("{err:?}")))?
[324](#324)            .len();
[325](#325)
[326](#326)            der.truncate(der_len);
[327](#327)
[328](#328)            return Ok(ControlFlow::Break(Some((kind, der))));
[329](#329)        }
[330](#330)    }
[331](#331)
[332](#332)    if section.is_some() {
[333](#333)        b64buf.extend(line);
[334](#334)        if b64buf.len() > MAX_PEM_SECTION_SIZE {
[335](#335)            return Err(Error::SectionTooLarge);
[336](#336)        }
[337](#337)    }
[338](#338)
[339](#339)    Ok(ControlFlow::Continue(()))
[340](#340)}

[529](#529)#[cfg(feature = "std")]
[532](#532)fn read_until_newline<R: io::BufRead + ?Sized>(r: &mut R, buf: &mut Vec<u8>) -> io::Result<usize> {
[533](#533)    let mut read = 0;
[534](#534)    loop {
[535](#535)        let (done, used) = {
[536](#536)            let available = match r.fill_buf() {
[537](#537)                Ok(n) => n,
[538](#538)                Err(ref e) if e.kind() == ErrorKind::Interrupted => continue,
[539](#539)                Err(e) => return Err(e),
[540](#540)            };
[541](#541)            match available
[542](#542)                .iter()
[543](#543)                .copied()
[544](#544)                .position(|b| b == b'\n' || b == b'\r')
[545](#545)            {
[546](#546)                Some(i) => {
[547](#547)                    buf.extend_from_slice(&available[..=i]);
[548](#548)                    (true, i + 1)
[549](#549)                }
[550](#550)                None => {
[551](#551)                    buf.extend_from_slice(available);
[552](#552)                    (false, available.len())
[553](#553)                }
[554](#554)            }
[555](#555)        };
[556](#556)        r.consume(used);
[557](#557)        read += used;
[558](#558)        if done || used == 0 {
[559](#559)            return Ok(read);
[560](#560)        }
[561](#561)    }

`alloc`## Expand description

Errors that may arise when parsing the contents of a PEM file

## Variants (Non-exhaustive)[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## This enum is marked as non-exhaustive

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MissingSectionEnd)

### MissingSectionEnd

a section is missing its “END marker” line

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.IllegalSectionStart)

### IllegalSectionStart

syntax error found in the line that starts a new section

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Base64Decode)

### Base64Decode([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

base64 decode error

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Io)

### Io([Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/io/error/struct.Error.html))

**crate feature**only.

`std`I/O errors, from APIs that accept `std::io` types.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.NoItemsFound)

### NoItemsFound

No items found of desired type

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SectionTooLarge)

### SectionTooLarge

PEM section exceeds maximum allowed size of 256 MB

# Zeroize in zeroize - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/1.8.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeroize/trait.Zeroize.html

```
pub trait Zeroize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[zeroize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.zeroize)(&mut self);
}## Expand description

Trait for securely erasing values from memory.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://docs.rs#foreign-impls)

This impl can eventually be optimized using an memset intrinsic,
such as [ core::intrinsics::volatile_set_memory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/intrinsics/fn.volatile_set_memory.html). For that reason the
blanket impl on slices is bounded by

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html)

`DefaultIsZeroes`To zeroize a mut slice of `Z: Zeroize` which does not impl
[ DefaultIsZeroes](https://docs.rs/trait.DefaultIsZeroes.html), call

`iter_mut().zeroize()`.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/zeroize/lib.rs.html#439-446)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Zeroize-for-MaybeUninit%3CZ%3E)### impl<Z> [Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) for [MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<Z>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/zeroize/lib.rs.html#439-446)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/zeroize/lib.rs.html#457-472)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Zeroize-for-%5BMaybeUninit%3CZ%3E%5D)### impl<Z> [Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) for [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<Z>]

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/zeroize/lib.rs.html#457-472)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Zeroize-for-%5BMaybeUninit%3CZ%3E%5D)

### impl<Z> [Zeroize](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroize.html) for [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html)<Z>]

This impl can eventually be optimized using an memset intrinsic,
such as [ core::intrinsics::volatile_set_memory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/intrinsics/fn.volatile_set_memory.html).

This fills the slice with zeroes.

Note that this ignore invariants that `Z` might have, because
[ MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html) removes all invariants.
